rw: The federal E-SIGN Act and state UETA give electronic signatures, including typed names and tablet signatures, the same legal effect as ink if the parties intended to sign electronically.

ww.No, tablets are illegal for signing cont: Tablets and other devices are routinely used to sign contracts, and E-SIGN specifically allows electronic signing, so no general ban on tablet signatures exists in contract law.
ww.No, only ink signatures count, so a type: This is outdated, since E-SIGN and UETA say a signature cannot be denied legal effect only because it is electronic, so a typed name can bind the signer.
ww.Only if notarized by a public notary and: Notarization and witnesses are required only for certain documents such as deeds or wills, not for an ordinary service contract, which can be validly formed without either.

rw: The implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, found in every contract, bars a party from acting to deprive the other of the benefits it reasonably expected, even without a written term.

ww.A duty to sign a second contract with th: Nothing in the implied covenant forces parties to sign a second contract; it only governs how each side performs and enforces the existing agreement, not future dealings.
ww.A duty to lower prices for customers who: Volume discounts are a matter of negotiated price terms; the implied covenant does not require sellers to cut prices for large buyers or set any pricing at all.
ww.A duty to give gifts to the other side a: The covenant concerns honest performance of the contract, not gifts; no party owes the other side presents after signing unless the contract itself says so.

rw: Under the common law mirror image rule, an acceptance must match the offer's terms exactly; any change is treated as a rejection and counteroffer, which UCC 2-207 relaxes for goods.

ww.Two contracts must be identical in every: The rule concerns whether the acceptance matches the offer, not whether two separate contracts are word-for-word identical, so it does not demand identical documents.
ww.An offer must be written in mirrors, so: The name is only a metaphor for matching terms; offers need not be written, and nothing about the rule involves mirrors or reading an offer back.
ww.A seller must copy the buyer's logo onto: The rule has nothing to do with logos or branding; it only compares the terms of the acceptance with the terms of the offer to decide if a contract formed.

rw: Under 2-207(2), a contract forms despite the added terms, which are treated as proposals that become part of the deal only if not material and not objected to by the offeror.

ww.Voids the offer permanently, so no contr: Under UCC 2-207, a definite acceptance with extra terms does not destroy the offer; the contract can still form, so the offer is not voided permanently.
ww.Never forms a contract between merchants: This is wrong because 2-207 was written to abandon the strict mirror image rule for goods, so an acceptance with added terms often does form a contract between merchants.
ww.Always replaces the original offer, what: The additional terms do not automatically replace the offer; they are only proposals, and between merchants they join the contract only if they are not material and the offeror does not object.

rw: UCC 2-205 makes a merchant's signed written offer irrevocable for the stated time, up to three months, without consideration, so the offeree can rely on it while shopping around.

ww.An offer made by a minor under the age o: This describes a minor's voidable offer, which is about capacity to contract; a firm offer under UCC 2-205 concerns merchants and keeping an offer open for a stated time.
ww.An offer that expires instantly when the: A firm offer does the opposite of expiring instantly; it is designed to stay open for the stated time, which is the purpose of UCC 2-205.
ww.An offer with no price, no goods and no: A valid offer needs reasonably definite terms, and a firm offer must state its assurance of staying open; one missing price, goods and date would not even be a valid offer.

rw: An option contract is a separate agreement, supported by consideration such as a fee, to keep an offer open for a set time so the offeror cannot revoke it meanwhile.

ww.A contract to sell stock only, at a fixe: An option contract is not limited to stock; it can cover real estate, goods or business sales, and its defining feature is keeping an offer open, not a stock sale date.
ww.A contract with no end date and no set t: An option contract does have a defined period during which the offer stays open, so the missing end date described here is the opposite of how options work.
ww.A contract about taxes owed by the buyer: Tax obligations between buyer and seller are governed by tax law and sale terms, and have no connection to an option contract, which concerns keeping an offer open.

rw: The $500 payment is consideration for holding the offer open for 60 days, making this an option contract; the seller cannot revoke or sell to others during that period.

ww.A rental lease: A lease gives temporary possession of property in exchange for rent, but here the buyer pays for the right to buy later, which is purchase rights, not occupancy.
ww.A gift of money: A gift involves no payment or exchange, but here the buyer pays $500 as consideration for the option, so the transaction is a bargained-for contract, not a gift.
ww.A void agreement: A void agreement has no legal effect, but this one has consideration and definite terms, so it is a valid, enforceable option contract.

rw: Under common law, an offeror may revoke at any time before acceptance, but options and UCC firm offers are exceptions because they are supported by consideration or statute.

ww.Only after acceptance has been given and: Once an offer is accepted, a contract has already formed and revocation is no longer possible; the question is about revoking before acceptance, so this is backwards.
ww.Only by a court order after both sides h: An offeror can revoke by simply notifying the offeree before acceptance; no court order or hearing is needed, because revocation is a private act of the offeror.
ww.Never, because an offer once made must s: Offers do not stay open forever; they end by lapse of time, rejection, revocation or death, and the offeror can generally withdraw before acceptance unless an option or firm offer applies.

rw: Silence can operate as acceptance only in limited cases, such as an established course of dealing between the parties or when the offeree accepts the benefit of services knowing payment is expected.

ww.Always, since silence is a clear sign of: Silence does not normally accept an offer, because an offeree has no duty to respond; treating all silence as agreement would let anyone force contracts on others.
ww.Never, since silence has no effect on an: This is too absolute because exceptions exist, such as prior dealings, an offeree who takes the benefit of services knowingly, or when the offeror's terms say silence means acceptance.
ww.Only on weekends, when the offer is open: Weekends and public offers have no special rule about silence; the exceptions depend on prior dealings, accepted benefits or agreed terms, not on the day of the week.

rw: Under UCC 2-601, the buyer may reject goods that fail in any respect to conform to the contract, though sellers often get a right to cure that softens the rule.

ww.A buyer must accept all goods delivered,: The perfect tender rule says the opposite: a buyer is not forced to accept goods that fail to conform, and may reject any delivery that does not match the contract.
ww.A seller may deliver any goods at all, w: The perfect tender rule protects the buyer, not the seller; a seller must deliver goods that conform to the contract rather than whatever it chooses.
ww.A seller may never deliver late, whateve: Late delivery is only one possible defect, and the rule is about nonconforming goods generally; sellers can sometimes cure a late or defective delivery within the contract time.

rw: Under the perfect tender rule, wrong-color mugs are nonconforming, so the buyer may reject the delivery, subject to the seller's right to cure within the time for performance.

ww.Keep them and pay nothing at all: The buyer is not entitled to keep nonconforming goods without paying; if the buyer accepts them, the price is owed, perhaps reduced by damages for the defect.
ww.Sue the delivery driver for it: The driver is only a carrier and not a party to the sale; the buyer's rights run against the seller, usually rejection, not a suit against the delivery driver.
ww.Force the seller to paint them: The buyer cannot force the seller to repaint the goods; the remedies are rejection, acceptance with damages or cover, while the seller may choose to cure by delivering red mugs.

rw: Under UCC 2-508, a seller who delivers nonconforming goods may notify the buyer and cure by replacing or fixing them within the original contract time, or sometimes longer.

ww.A right to double the price of the goods: Right to cure gives the seller a chance to fix the problem, not a right to raise prices; a late delivery does not let the seller charge double.
ww.A right to refuse payment for the goods: Right to cure does not let a seller refuse payment; it protects the seller by letting them correct a defective delivery so the buyer must still accept and pay.
ww.A right to cancel the contract if the go: Cure is the opposite of cancellation; it lets the seller repair or replace a bad delivery to save the contract, not end the contract because goods are late.

rw: Under UCC 2-712, the buyer may buy substitute goods in good faith after a seller's breach and recover the difference between the cover price and the contract price, plus incidental damages.

ww.A late fee charged to a buyer who pays t: A late fee is a charge for slow payment, not a buyer's remedy; cover is what a buyer does after the seller fails to deliver.
ww.Hiding a defect from the buyer so that i: Concealing a defect is fraud or misrepresentation, not a remedy; cover is a lawful remedy the buyer uses after the seller breaches by not delivering.
ww.Covering the goods with plastic sheets t: Physically covering goods is unrelated to the legal term; cover as a buyer's remedy means buying replacement goods when the seller fails to deliver or delivers goods that were rejected.

rw: Cover damages equal the cover price minus the contract price: ($13 - $10) x 200 units = $3 x 200 = $600, plus any incidental damages, if any.

ww.$2,000: This is the original contract price of 200 x $10 = $2,000, which the buyer would have paid anyway, and not the extra cost of buying substitutes.
ww.$200: This figure does not match any step of the calculation; the extra cost per unit is $3, and multiplying by 200 units gives a much larger amount.
ww.$2,600: This is the total substitute purchase cost of 200 x $13 = $2,600, but cover damages only recover the difference over the contract price, not the whole price.

rw: Under UCC 2-608, a buyer who accepted goods may revoke acceptance when a defect substantially impairs their value and was hidden or the buyer reasonably relied on the seller's assurances.

ww.A refund of shipping only, with no refun: Revocation of acceptance is not a shipping refund; it lets the buyer undo an acceptance of goods and recover the price paid, not just delivery costs.
ww.A tax form that the buyer must file with: Revocation of acceptance is a contract remedy under UCC 2-608, not a tax filing; the state does not require a form when goods are returned.
ww.A seller's right to cancel a sale after: Revocation of acceptance belongs to the buyer, not the seller; a seller cannot cancel a completed sale after delivery just because the buyer has accepted the goods.

rw: Under UCC Article 7, a warehouse receipt is a document of title issued by a warehouse, confirming it holds the stated goods, and it can be transferred to pass ownership.

ww.A receipt for a rent payment made to a l: Rent payments to a landlord are acknowledged by a rent receipt; a warehouse receipt concerns stored goods, not leases or payments of rent.
ww.A tax invoice for goods stored in a ware: A tax invoice records a sale and amounts owed; a warehouse receipt is a document of title that proves goods are stored, and it does not bill the owner for tax.
ww.A letter to customers about goods held i: A warehouse receipt is not a letter to customers; it is a formal document of title that can be negotiated and transferred to give the holder rights to the stored goods.

rw: Under UCC 2-702 and 2-705, a seller who discovers a buyer is insolvent before delivery may refuse to deliver except for cash and may stop goods in transit.

ww.To cancel without notice always: The seller cannot always cancel without notice; the UCC lets the seller refuse credit terms or stop delivery, but other rules and notice requirements still apply.
ww.To demand twice the price paid: Twice the price would be a windfall; remedies for an insolvent buyer protect the seller from nonpayment and do not give damages beyond the actual contract price.
ww.To sue the carrier for the loss: The carrier did not cause the loss; the seller's protection comes from refusing credit or stopping delivery, not from suing a carrier that merely transports the goods.

rw: The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act of 1975 governs written warranties on consumer products, requiring clear disclosure of terms and labeling warranties as full or limited.

ww.Zoning rules for land used by shops: Zoning is regulated by local governments under land use law, and the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act has nothing to do with where shops may be located.
ww.Stock offerings made by small firms: Securities offerings by small firms are regulated by the SEC under securities laws, not by the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, which covers consumer warranties.
ww.Employment contracts on pay and hours: Employment pay and hours are covered by laws such as the Fair Labor Standards Act, while Magnuson-Moss deals only with consumer product warranties.

rw: Under Magnuson-Moss, a full warranty must provide repair or replacement without charge within a reasonable time, while a limited warranty gives less and must be clearly labeled limited.

ww.A limited warranty has no terms and give: A limited warranty still has terms and remedies; the Act only requires that a limited warranty be clearly labeled, so saying it gives the buyer no rights is wrong.
ww.They are identical in every way and give: The two are not identical; a full warranty carries minimum federal standards, such as free repair, that a limited warranty need not meet.
ww.A full warranty lasts only one day, whil: Full and limited do not refer to how long a warranty lasts; the labels describe the strength of the remedies, and either type can last for different periods.

rw: Advertising a lifetime guarantee while the written warranty excludes most defects can mislead consumers, raising deceptive advertising concerns under FTC rules and the Magnuson-Moss Act.

ww.A zoning issue concerning where the busi: Zoning concerns land use, and location of the business has no bearing on whether a warranty is advertised accurately or fully disclosed to consumers.
ww.An antitrust issue concerning competitio: Antitrust law concerns competition and monopolies, but the issue here is the gap between an advertised guarantee and the actual written warranty, which affects consumers.
ww.A trademark issue only, with no effect o: Trademark law protects brand identity, and the misleading guarantee here deceives consumers, so the issue is not trademark only and consumers are clearly affected.

rw: The CAN-SPAM Act requires commercial emails to include a working opt-out method, accurate header and sender information, truthful subject lines, and a valid physical postal address for the sender.

ww.That emails contain no links to any othe: CAN-SPAM does not ban links; legitimate marketing emails routinely include links, and the law targets deceptive headers, missing opt-outs and misleading subject lines.
ww.That all emails be encrypted before they: Encryption is not required by CAN-SPAM; the law is about honesty and opt-out rights, not about the technical security of messages in transit.
ww.That emails be sent only at night, when: CAN-SPAM sets no time of day restriction on email; its rules cover truthful content and opt-out handling, unlike some telemarketing rules that limit calling hours.

rw: COPPA requires websites and apps directed at children under 13 to get verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information, and the FTC enforces it.

ww.Imports of goods from other countries: Imports are regulated by customs and trade law, and COPPA, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, has nothing to do with goods from other countries.
ww.Pets kept as animals in homes and farms: Animals and pets are covered by animal welfare and property laws, while COPPA concerns the online collection of personal information from young children.
ww.Employees' wages and hours under labor l: Employee pay and hours are governed by labor laws such as the FLSA, but COPPA protects children's personal information online, not worker wages.

rw: COPPA bars collecting personal information, such as names and locations, from children under 13 without verifiable parental consent, which the app violated by collecting data from 9-year-olds.

ww.OSHA: OSHA covers workplace safety and health, and it has no role in how a game app collects personal data from children online.
ww.FLSA: The FLSA governs minimum wage, overtime and child labor in employment, not the collection of children's personal information by an online game.
ww.TILA: TILA, the Truth in Lending Act, requires credit cost disclosures and has no connection to a game app collecting data from children.

rw: The National Do Not Call Registry, run by the FTC, lets consumers opt out of most telemarketing calls, and businesses must stop calling numbers listed on it.

ww.Register businesses that sell goods by p: The registry lists consumer phone numbers that telemarketers should not call, not businesses that sell by phone, so it works in the opposite direction.
ww.Raise phone prices charged to the consum: The registry has no effect on phone prices; it only restricts telemarketing calls to registered numbers, and it does not regulate carrier rates.
ww.Ban all phone calls made by any business: The registry does not ban all calls; exemptions exist for political calls, charities, surveys and companies with an existing business relationship with the consumer.

rw: Created by the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, the CFPB protects consumers in financial products and services such as mortgages, credit cards, student loans and debt collection.

ww.Prints money and coins for use by banks: The U.S. Mint and the Bureau of Engraving and Printing produce coins and paper money, while the CFPB supervises financial products such as loans, cards and mortgages.
ww.Sets the federal budget and how much the: The federal budget is set by Congress and the President; the CFPB regulates consumer financial products and has no role in setting state or federal spending.
ww.Runs the stock market and sets prices fo: The SEC regulates securities markets and the exchanges set share prices through trading, while the CFPB focuses on consumer lending and financial services.

rw: Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card use is capped at $50, and many issuers even offer zero liability policies.

ww.$500: A $500 cap is not the typical limit for reported credit card fraud; it resembles older rules for certain unreported debit card losses, not this timely credit card report.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 does not match any federal liability cap; the law limits credit card losses far below this amount when fraud is reported promptly.
ww.$5,000: $5,000 is not a federal cap on credit card fraud liability; the law limits the cardholder's loss to $50 at most for unauthorized charges.

rw: A holder in due course takes a negotiable instrument for value, in good faith and without notice of defects or dishonor, and gets stronger rights than ordinary holders.

ww.A person who steals the instrument and t: A thief took the instrument unlawfully and did not give value in good faith, so a thief cannot be a holder in due course regardless of cashing it.
ww.A person who receives it as a gift from: Taking an instrument as a gift involves no value given, and value is required, so a donee does not qualify as a holder in due course.
ww.A person who knows it is forged but take: Knowledge that an instrument is forged defeats good faith and the no-notice requirement, so someone who takes it knowingly cannot be a holder in due course.

rw: A holder in due course takes free of most personal defenses such as breach of warranty or defective goods, so the buyer must still pay the bank and pursue the seller instead.

ww.Required to be paid twice, to the seller: The buyer is not required to pay twice; the buyer pays the holder in due course and then claims against the seller for the defective goods.
ww.Fully valid against the bank, whatever t: Personal defenses like defective goods are generally not valid against a holder in due course, so saying they are fully valid against the bank is wrong.
ww.Automatic cancellation of the note for t: A defense of defective goods does not automatically cancel the note, especially once a holder in due course owns it; the buyer's remedy lies against the seller.

rw: Real defenses, such as forgery, fraud in the factum, infancy, duress and bankruptcy discharge, are valid against everyone including a holder in due course.

ww.A late delivery of the goods to the buye: Late delivery of goods is a personal defense, such as breach of contract, which a holder in due course takes free of, so it does not defeat payment.
ww.A dislike of the product shown by the bu: Dislike of a product is a personal complaint and not a legal defense at all; real defenses involve serious problems like forgery or incapacity.
ww.A complaint about the price paid by the: A complaint about price is a personal defense, such as failure of consideration or a bad bargain, and cannot be raised against a holder in due course.

rw: Under UCC 4-403, a customer may order the bank not to pay a particular check before it is paid, usually in writing or by phone, and may owe a fee.

ww.An order to raise a limit on the amount: Raising a spending limit is a different banking instruction; a stop-payment order cancels payment of a specific check and does not alter limits on spending.
ww.An order to print a statement for a cust: Requests for statements are routine account services, while a stop-payment order is an instruction to the bank not to pay a particular check.
ww.An order to close an account and send th: Closing an account and withdrawing funds is a different instruction; a stop-payment order only stops payment of one particular check, without closing anything.

rw: A stop-payment order tells the bank not to pay the check, which protects the customer if goods never arrived, as long as it is placed before the check clears.

ww.Do nothing and hope the problem goes awa: Doing nothing lets the check clear and the funds leave the account, leaving the customer to recover money from the store later with more difficulty.
ww.Mail the check back to the store only: Mailing the check back to the store does not stop it from being cashed or deposited, and the bank may still pay it if it is presented.
ww.Pay twice to be safe with the store: Paying twice only multiplies the customer's loss; a stop-payment order is the proper step to prevent payment on an uncleared check for undelivered goods.

rw: A cashier's check is drawn by the bank on its own funds, with the bank as both drawer and drawee, so it is considered nearly as good as cash.

ww.A personal check on a closed bank accoun: A check on a closed account is a worthless personal check that will be dishonored, while a cashier's check is backed by the bank's own funds.
ww.A check with no signature on its face: An unsigned check is not valid, since a negotiable instrument requires a signature; a cashier's check is signed by a bank officer and drawn on the bank.
ww.A check written by a store clerk by hand: A cashier's check is issued by a bank, not written by hand by a store clerk, and the purchaser pays the bank for the amount first.

rw: A certified check is a customer's check that the drawee bank has guaranteed by marking it certified and setting aside the funds, so the bank becomes primarily liable on it.

ww.A check with a certificate of origin att: A certified check is certified by the bank on which it is drawn, not by a foreign bank, and no certificate of origin is involved.
ww.A rubber check that bounces when the ban: A bounced check is called a dishonored or bad check, and a certified check is the reverse since the bank has promised to pay it.
ww.A check approved by a customer before it: Customer approval does not make a check certified; the bank itself must accept and certify the check, which guarantees that funds are held to pay it.

rw: A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, so payment depends on the bank rather than the unknown buyer, though verifying the bank avoids counterfeit risk.

ww.A personal check from an unknown buyer: A personal check from an unknown buyer may bounce, and the seller bears that risk, so it offers little security for a large payment.
ww.An unsigned note from an unknown buyer: An unsigned note is not even a valid negotiable instrument and gives the seller no enforceable promise from an unknown buyer.
ww.A promise to pay later, signed by the bu: A promise to pay later carries the buyer's credit risk, so the seller may not be paid if the unknown buyer fails to pay.

rw: Forgery means signing another person's name, or altering an instrument, without authority, and a forged signature generally has no effect as that person's signature.

ww.Depositing a check that is made out to y: Depositing a check made out to you is a proper, lawful act, with no signature falsified, so it is not forgery in any sense.
ww.Endorsing your own check by signing the: Endorsing your own check by signing the back is the normal, lawful way to cash or deposit it, and it involves no false signature.
ww.Voiding a check before it is cashed by t: Voiding a check means canceling it before payment, which the drawer may lawfully do, and it does not involve falsely signing someone's name.

rw: The Electronic Fund Transfer Act protects consumers using electronic transfers such as debit cards, ATMs and direct deposits, and limits their liability for unauthorized use.

ww.Patents and trademarks held by firms and: Patents and trademarks are protected by intellectual property laws, while the Electronic Fund Transfer Act concerns consumers' electronic banking transactions.
ww.Employees' wages and the overtime hours: Employee wages and overtime fall under the Fair Labor Standards Act, whereas the Electronic Fund Transfer Act covers electronic payments by consumers.
ww.Imports and the duties that are charged: Imports and duties are handled by customs and tariff laws, while the Electronic Fund Transfer Act governs consumer electronic payments such as debit card and ATM use.

rw: Under the EFTA, reporting a lost or stolen debit card within two business days caps the consumer's liability for unauthorized use at $50.

ww.$500: $500 is the cap when a consumer reports a lost debit card after two business days but within sixty days, not when it is reported promptly.
ww.$250: $250 is not a limit set by the EFTA; the law uses $50, $500 or unlimited liability depending on how quickly the consumer reports the loss.
ww.$5,000: $5,000 is not an EFTA liability cap; the statute limits prompt reporters to $50, with larger exposure only if the consumer waits much longer.

rw: The business judgment rule presumes directors acted informed, in good faith and in the company's interest, so courts generally will not second-guess their decisions absent fraud or conflicts.

ww.A rule on employee pay and the benefits: Employee pay and benefits are covered by employment law, while the business judgment rule shields directors from liability for informed, good-faith business decisions.
ww.A rule that directors must always profit: Directors owe duties of care and loyalty to the corporation; they are not guaranteed profit, and the rule protects reasonable decisions even if they lose money.
ww.A rule banning directors from taking any: The rule does not ban risk; directors may take reasonable business risks, and courts defer to their informed, good-faith judgment rather than penalize losses.

rw: An informed, good-faith decision made in the company's interest is protected by the business judgment rule, even though the new market lost money for the corporation.

ww.Removed by the court: Courts do not remove directors merely because a good-faith, informed decision lost money; removal requires misconduct such as breach of loyalty or fraud.
ww.Required to repay all losses: The directors are not required to repay losses from an honest business decision, because the rule protects reasonable choices, even those that turn out badly.
ww.Automatically liable: Directors are not automatically liable for bad outcomes; liability needs a breach of duty, such as bad faith or lack of information, not merely a loss.

rw: In a derivative suit, a shareholder sues on the corporation's behalf against insiders or third parties who harmed it, and any recovery goes to the corporation.

ww.A suit on a derivative stock held by a t: Derivative securities such as options relate to financial trading, while a derivative lawsuit is a shareholder suit brought on behalf of the corporation.
ww.A suit by employees for unpaid wages, br: Unpaid wage claims belong to employees under labor law and are not derivative suits, which are brought by shareholders for the corporation's benefit.
ww.A suit by a customer against a store ove: A customer suing over a faulty product brings a product liability claim for personal injury or loss, not a shareholder derivative suit on the corporation's behalf.

rw: A proxy lets a shareholder authorize another person to vote her shares at a meeting, which is common when owners cannot attend in person.

ww.A fee paid to attend meetings of the sha: Shareholders are not charged to attend meetings, and a proxy is a grant of voting authority, not an admission fee paid at the door.
ww.A type of stock split that gives each ho: A stock split increases the number of shares without changing ownership value, while a proxy is a delegation of voting authority to another person.
ww.A legal fine imposed on a firm by the st: A fine imposed by the state would be a penalty, while a proxy is a voluntary authorization for another person to vote the shares.

rw: Cumulative voting lets a shareholder multiply shares by open seats and put all votes on one or a few candidates, helping minority shareholders win board representation.

ww.A system for officers only, where shareh: In cumulative voting shareholders do vote for directors, and the system exists to help minority holders, so saying they cannot vote is wrong.
ww.A system banning voting for shareholders: Cumulative voting is a way of voting at meetings, not a ban on voting, and it is intended to give small shareholders more influence.
ww.A system of one vote per director, so th: That describes the opposite, since cumulative voting allows votes to be pooled behind one person, while straight voting restricts votes to one per share per seat.

rw: Under cumulative voting, total votes equal shares times seats: 100 x 3 = 300, and she may cast all 300 for a single candidate.

ww.3: 3 would be the number of seats and not the number of votes; votes equal shares times seats, so the total is much larger.
ww.33: 33 does not fit; dividing 100 shares by 3 seats has no role in the formula, since votes are multiplied by the seats rather than divided.
ww.100: 100 is her share count, but cumulative voting gives her 100 x 3 seats = 300 votes, all of which she may cast for one candidate.

rw: In a merger, two corporations combine and one survives, absorbing the other's assets and liabilities, while the other corporation ceases to exist.

ww.A tax audit of a firm carried out by the: A tax audit is a government review of a firm's returns and has nothing to do with the legal combination of two corporations.
ww.A split of one company into many smaller: Splitting one company into many smaller firms is a breakup, divestiture or spinoff, which is the opposite of a merger.
ww.A loan between firms to cover short-term: A loan between firms is a financing arrangement and does not combine the companies, which is what a merger does.

rw: In a hostile takeover the acquirer goes around management, often by a tender offer to shareholders or a proxy fight, to gain control against its wishes.

ww.A strike by workers who stop work in ord: A strike is a labor action by workers, and a hostile takeover is a corporate acquisition, so the two concepts are unrelated.
ww.A friendly merger agreed by the boards o: A friendly merger approved by both boards is the opposite of hostile; a takeover is hostile when the target's management resists the acquirer.
ww.A product recall ordered by a regulator: A product recall is a safety action ordered by a regulator or firm, and it has nothing to do with acquiring control of a company.

rw: Dissolution is the legal end of a corporation's existence, followed by winding up its affairs, paying debts and distributing remaining assets to shareholders.

ww.A change of logo and of the company name: A rebrand changes a logo or name but the corporation continues to exist, while dissolution ends its legal existence completely.
ww.A stock split of shares into more units: A stock split divides shares into more units without ending the company, so it does not dissolve the corporation in any way.
ww.The start of a corporation by its founde: Forming a corporation is incorporation, the opposite of dissolution, which closes the corporation down and ends its legal existence.

rw: On dissolution, creditors are paid first from the corporation's assets, and only what remains goes to shareholders, with preferred stockholders ahead of common stockholders.

ww.The founders: Founders have no special claim at dissolution unless they are also creditors or shareholders, and they are paid after debts are settled.
ww.Executives: Executives are paid as employees or creditors only for amounts owed, and they have no priority claim over creditors on dissolution.
ww.Stockholders: Stockholders are residual owners and are paid last, after all creditors, because they bear the risk of the business; only leftover assets go to them.

rw: A registered agent is a person or company designated to receive legal documents, such as service of process and official notices, on behalf of a business entity.

ww.A stock broker who buys and sells shares: A stockbroker buys and sells securities for clients and has no role in receiving legal papers for the business.
ww.A tax auditor who checks a company's boo: A tax auditor reviews financial records for a government agency, which differs from a registered agent who receives service of process for the company.
ww.A shareholder who owns part of a company: A shareholder owns part of the company and votes on its decisions, which is a different role from the registered agent who receives legal papers.

rw: A DBA, or assumed name, filing registers a trade name different from the owner's legal name, so the public can identify the real person behind the business.

ww.A bank loan taken out by the owner to st: A bank loan is financing and not a registration; a DBA filing simply records a business name that differs from the owner's legal name.
ww.A product license that lets a firm sell: A license to sell under another brand is a trademark or franchise arrangement, while a DBA filing only registers a business name.
ww.A tax deduction claimed by a business fo: A cost of goods sold deduction is a tax accounting item, which has no connection to registering a trade name as a DBA.

rw: A sole proprietor using a name other than her legal name usually must register a DBA or fictitious business name with the state or county.

ww.Articles of incorporation filed to form: Articles of incorporation are filed to form a corporation, but Maria runs a sole proprietorship under an assumed name and does not need one.
ww.A trade secret filing with the patent of: Trade secrets are protected by keeping information confidential and are not filed with the patent office, so this does not apply to Maria's business name.
ww.A patent application filed for an invent: A patent protects an invention, while Maria is using a business name, so a patent application is unrelated to her situation.

rw: A benefit corporation is a for-profit company that must also pursue a stated public benefit, and directors weigh the effects on society and stakeholders as well as shareholders.

ww.A union of workers who bargain with the: A union is an organization of workers who bargain with employers, whereas a benefit corporation is a for-profit company with a stated public benefit purpose.
ww.A corporation that pays no taxes of any: Benefit corporations still pay taxes like other for-profit corporations; their public purpose does not exempt them from taxation, unlike some nonprofits.
ww.A government agency that regulates the t: A government agency regulates commerce, but a benefit corporation is a private company that voluntarily commits to social goals alongside profit.

rw: A cooperative is owned and democratically controlled by its members, who use its services or buy its goods, and profits are shared among members.

ww.A business owned by the government that: A government-owned business is a public enterprise, while a cooperative is owned and controlled democratically by its member users.
ww.A business owned by one person who also: A business owned by one person who keeps all profits describes a sole proprietorship, not a cooperative, which has many member owners.
ww.A business with no members that is run o: A cooperative has members who own it and vote, so a business with no members run only by a hired manager does not fit.

rw: Agents owe principals fiduciary duties of loyalty, obedience, reasonable care and accounting, meaning they must act in the principal's interest and report on money handled.

ww.No duties at all owed to the principal: Agents owe several fiduciary duties because they act for the principal, so saying they owe none contradicts basic agency law.
ww.A duty to compete with the principal: An agent must avoid conflicts of interest and not compete with the principal, which is the opposite of owing a duty to compete.
ww.Only the duty to be paid, nothing else: Beyond being paid, an agent owes loyalty, obedience, care and accounting; pay is a right of the agent, not the agent's only duty.

rw: Secretly buying and reselling to the client at a markup puts her own interest ahead of the client's, which breaches the fiduciary duty of loyalty.

ww.Advertising: Advertising is not a standard fiduciary duty of agents; the issue is her secret self-dealing, which conflicts with the duty of loyalty.
ww.Tax duty: Tax duty is not an agent's core duty here; the misconduct is secret self-dealing and profit at the client's expense, which violates loyalty.
ww.Obedience: Obedience means following the principal's lawful instructions, but the problem here is self-dealing and secret profit, which is a breach of loyalty.

rw: A principal must pay agreed compensation, reimburse the agent's expenses, indemnify for losses and generally provide a reasonably safe working environment.

ww.No duties at all owed to the agent by th: A principal owes the agent duties such as compensation and reimbursement, so claiming there are no duties ignores the principal's obligations in agency law.
ww.A duty to give company stock to the agen: Giving stock is not a standard duty; stock is given only if the parties agreed to it in the contract.
ww.A duty to sell the business to the agent: Selling the business to the agent is not a legal duty; the principal owes pay, reimbursement and safe conditions, not a transfer of ownership.

rw: With an undisclosed principal, the third party does not know a principal exists and thinks the agent is acting for herself, though the principal can often still be bound.

ww.A principal who hides money from the age: An undisclosed principal's concealment concerns the third party not knowing the principal exists, not hiding money from the agent or anyone else.
ww.A principal who cannot be sued by any th: An undisclosed principal can be sued; once discovered, the third party may sue either the principal or the agent on the contract.
ww.A principal with no agent working for th: An undisclosed principal does have an agent acting on his behalf with authority, but the third party simply does not know the principal exists.

rw: An agency ends by mutual agreement, completion of the purpose, revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, or the death or incapacity of a party.

ww.Only by a tax filing made with the reven: Agency does not end through a tax filing; it ends through agreement, completion of the task, revocation, renunciation or the death or incapacity of a party.
ww.Only by lawsuit brought in a court of la: A lawsuit is not required to end an agency; either party can usually end it by notice, completion or other events without going to court.
ww.It can never end once it begins, whateve: Agency can always be ended by the principal's revocation or the agent's renunciation, though the party who ends it wrongly may owe damages.

rw: Apparent authority can linger when the principal fails to notify third parties who relied on past dealings, so the principal may still be bound by the agent's contract.

ww.The statute of frauds rule: The statute of frauds concerns which contracts must be in writing and does not decide whether a former agent can bind the principal.
ww.Express authority alone applies: Express authority was withdrawn when she told the agent to stop, so only the lingering appearance of authority to the unaware vendor can bind her.
ww.Nothing, as notice is not needed: Notice matters because third parties who dealt with the agent before may reasonably rely on apparent authority until told otherwise, so the principal can still be bound.

rw: The scope of employment is the range of activities an employee is hired or authorized to do, and employers are liable for torts committed within it.

ww.The company's total revenue earned durin: Total revenue is a financial figure for the company, whereas scope of employment is about which activities an employee is authorized to perform.
ww.The employee's home address on file with: The employee's home address is a payroll record that has no bearing on which activities fall within the job or on employer liability.
ww.The employee's pay raise at the end of e: A pay raise is a compensation matter, not a measure of the activities the employee is authorized to perform in the job.

rw: A personal day trip is typically outside the scope of employment, so respondeat superior usually does not apply and the employer is probably not liable, though negligent entrustment can matter.

ww.Liable only for tickets and parking fine: Fines and tickets may be personal to the driver, but employer liability for a crash depends on scope of employment, not on a narrow category of charges.
ww.Liable only if the car is red, whatever: The color of the vehicle has no legal relevance; the employer's liability depends on whether the employee was acting within the scope of employment.
ww.Always liable for everything the employe: Employers are not always liable; respondeat superior covers acts within the scope of employment, while a purely personal trip may fall outside it.

rw: Two or more businesses that share control over a worker's pay, hours or conditions are joint employers, and each can be liable for wage and hour violations.

ww.A worker who has two names, one used at: A joint employer is not a person with two names; it describes separate businesses that share control over the terms of a worker's employment.
ww.A tax preparer who files returns for cli: A tax preparer files returns for clients and is not an employer; a joint employer is a business sharing control over a worker.
ww.A union leader who negotiates pay on beh: A union leader bargains for members and is not an employer; a joint employer is an actual business that shares control of workers.

rw: The ABC test presumes a worker is an employee unless the hiring firm proves control freedom, work outside its usual business and an independent trade.

ww.Tests building codes for homes and shops: Building codes are set by local governments and inspected by building officials, not tested by the ABC test used for worker classification.
ww.Tests reading skills for students in pri: Reading skills for students are assessed by education tests, and the ABC test is a legal standard for classifying workers, not for schools.
ww.Tests stock prices for firms listed on t: Stock prices are set by market trading, and the ABC test is not related to finance; it is a legal test of worker status.

rw: A security deposit is money a tenant pays up front to cover potential damage or unpaid rent, and it is generally returned if the unit is left in good condition.

ww.A fine for moving out of the rented home: A fine for early move-out is a termination or breach penalty, while a security deposit is refundable money held to cover damage or unpaid rent.
ww.A gift to the landlord when a tenant mov: A security deposit is not a gift to the landlord; it is refundable money held to cover damage or unpaid rent beyond normal wear.
ww.A tax on rent paid by the tenant to the: A tax on rent is a government charge, but a security deposit is held by the landlord and is generally refundable to the tenant.

rw: Most states let landlords deduct only for damage beyond normal wear and tear, such as unpaid rent or real damage, so keeping the full deposit for faded paint is generally not allowed.

ww.Always allowed by the law: Landlords may deduct only for unpaid rent and damage beyond normal wear and tear, so always being allowed to keep the deposit is incorrect.
ww.Required in every state: No state requires landlords to keep the whole deposit, and statutes generally require refunding amounts not tied to damage or unpaid rent.
ww.A tax benefit for owners: Wrongfully retaining a deposit is not a tax benefit; it can expose the landlord to liability, including penalties in some states.

rw: The implied warranty of habitability requires landlords to keep rental housing safe and livable, with working heat, water, electricity and structure, and tenants cannot waive it in most states.

ww.A duty to lower rent whenever the tenant: The warranty of habitability concerns safe and livable housing, not rent reductions on request, though tenants may get remedies if a landlord fails to repair.
ww.A landlord's duty to buy furniture for t: Landlords generally need not furnish furniture unless the lease says so; the warranty covers basic safety and livability of the unit.
ww.A tenant's duty to decorate the rental u: The warranty places duties on landlords, not tenants to decorate, and it covers safe, livable conditions for tenants.

rw: Eviction is the legal process a landlord uses to remove a tenant, usually requiring notice and a court order, and self-help removal is generally unlawful.

ww.A repair request sent by a tenant to the: A written repair request is a tenant's notice about maintenance and is not a process for removing a tenant from the property.
ww.A rent increase announced by the landlor: A rent increase is a change in lease terms, and does not remove the tenant from the property as eviction does.
ww.A lease renewal signed by the tenant and: A lease renewal extends the tenancy, which is the opposite of eviction, which ends the tenant's right to occupy.

rw: Changing locks without a court order is an illegal self-help eviction in most states, and landlords may owe damages to the tenant.

ww.A lawful eviction by the landlord: A lawful eviction requires notice and a court order, so locking out a tenant without either is not lawful.
ww.A rent adjustment by the landlord: A rent adjustment changes the amount charged and does not involve excluding the tenant from the rental unit.
ww.A routine repair by the landlord: Changing locks is not a repair; a repair fixes defects, but here the landlord is removing the tenant's access without legal process.

rw: A deed is a written, signed legal document that transfers ownership of real property from the grantor to the grantee and is usually recorded.

ww.A mortgage payment made to the lender ea: A mortgage payment goes to the lender to repay a loan, while a deed is the document that transfers ownership of real property.
ww.A zoning map showing how land is used in: A zoning map shows permitted land uses, whereas a deed is the document that transfers title between owners.
ww.A rent receipt given by the landlord to: A rent receipt only proves a rent payment, while a deed transfers ownership of real estate itself.

rw: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the grantor has, if any, without warranties or guarantees of clear title, and is often used between family members or to clear title defects.

ww.A deed that guarantees clear title to th: A deed guaranteeing clear title with warranties is a warranty deed, whereas a quitclaim deed gives no promises about title.
ww.A deed that sells a car or other motor v: A car sale is transferred by a certificate of title, not a deed, and a quitclaim deed deals with real property interests.
ww.A deed that cancels a mortgage and relea: Canceling a mortgage and releasing a lien is done by a satisfaction or release of mortgage, which is a different document than a quitclaim deed.

rw: A general warranty deed gives the broadest protection, as the grantor promises clear title against all defects, including those arising before the grantor's ownership.

ww.A quitclaim deed only: A quitclaim deed gives no warranties about title, so it is the weakest protection and the least suitable for a buyer wanting security.
ww.No deed is required: A deed is needed to transfer title to real property, so skipping one would leave the buyer without legal ownership.
ww.A lease of the land: A lease grants temporary possession rather than ownership, so it gives no protection of clear title.

rw: Title insurance protects a buyer or lender against losses from defects in a property's title, such as liens, forgery or errors in public records.

ww.Insurance against fire damage to the pro: Fire damage is covered by property or hazard insurance, whereas title insurance protects against defects in the title to the property.
ww.Insurance on a car that covers damage fr: Auto insurance covers vehicles and has no connection to the ownership defects that title insurance covers in real estate.
ww.Insurance on a job that pays workers whe: Lost wages from work injuries are covered by workers' compensation, which is a different insurance from title insurance on real property.

rw: Zoning is a set of local government rules controlling how land can be used, such as residential, commercial or industrial zones, and what may be built.

ww.A survey tool used to measure the size o: Surveys measure the size and boundaries of land, while zoning is the set of local rules controlling land use.
ww.A type of loan used to buy a home or oth: A home loan is a mortgage, while zoning is a set of local government rules on how land may be used.
ww.A tax on land charged by the local gover: A tax on land is a property tax, and zoning is instead a land use regulation that sets what may be built where.

rw: A factory in a residential zone breaks the zoning rules, so the business would need a variance or rezoning approval from the local authority.

ww.A trademark registration filed for the f: A trademark protects brand identity and does not authorize a particular land use, so it cannot allow a factory in a residential zone.
ww.Nothing, as the land is private property: Private ownership does not override zoning law, so the business cannot use the land for any purpose it wants without approval.
ww.A patent application for the factory: A patent protects an invention and does not affect where the factory may be located or what zoning allows.

rw: An easement is a right to use another person's land for a limited purpose, such as a utility line or a shared driveway, without owning it.

ww.A tax break for homeowners who pay inter: A mortgage interest deduction is a tax rule, while an easement is a right to use another's land for a limited purpose.
ww.A type of mortgage with fixed payments f: A fixed-rate mortgage is a loan; an easement is a property right and has nothing to do with loan payments.
ww.A building permit issued by the city for: A building permit is government permission to build, while an easement is a property right to use another's land for a limited purpose.

rw: Adverse possession lets someone gain title by occupying land openly, continuously, exclusively and hostilely for the statutory period, often 10 to 20 years, depending on the state.

ww.Renting land from the owner for a fixed: Renting under a lease is a permissive use with payments, whereas adverse possession is occupying land openly without the owner's consent.
ww.Buying land at an auction held by the lo: Buying land at auction transfers title by purchase, whereas adverse possession gains title through long, open occupation without consent.
ww.Stealing a car from a parking lot in the: Stealing a car is a crime about personal property and not adverse possession, which concerns acquiring real estate title by occupation.

rw: Under comparative negligence, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault, so a partly at-fault plaintiff recovers less but may still recover something.

ww.A rule on rent and the amounts that land: Rent rules belong to landlord-tenant law, whereas comparative negligence is a tort rule allocating fault between plaintiff and defendant.
ww.A rule that bans suits against any firm: Comparative negligence does not ban suits; it allows partly at-fault plaintiffs to recover reduced damages instead of being barred.
ww.A rule that doubles damages if the plain: Comparative negligence reduces damages for the plaintiff's fault and never doubles them, so a partly at-fault plaintiff gets less.

rw: Her damages are reduced by her 30% fault: $50,000 x 0.30 = $15,000, and $50,000 - $15,000 = $35,000, which she recovers.

ww.$15,000: $15,000 is 30% of $50,000, which is the amount of the reduction, not what she recovers.
ww.$5,000: $5,000 does not match the calculation; 30% of $50,000 is $15,000, so the recovery is $35,000.
ww.$50,000: $50,000 ignores her fault; comparative negligence reduces the award by 30%, so she cannot recover the full amount.

rw: Assumption of risk is a defense that can bar or reduce recovery when the plaintiff knew of and voluntarily accepted the danger that caused the injury.

ww.A form of insurance covering injuries th: Insurance for risky activities is a different matter, while assumption of risk is a defense used when a plaintiff knowingly accepted the danger.
ww.A tax rule on the amount of income that: A tax rule on income is unrelated; assumption of risk is a tort defense to liability based on the plaintiff's knowing acceptance of danger.
ww.A contract term on rent and the dates of: A rent payment term is a contract provision, and assumption of risk is instead a defense to tort liability and not a lease term.

rw: Premises liability makes owners responsible for injuries caused by unsafe conditions they knew or should have known about, and a duty depends on whether the visitor is an invitee, licensee or trespasser.

ww.A tenant's duty to pay rent on time and: That describes a tenant's duties under a lease, whereas premises liability concerns an owner's responsibility for injuries from unsafe conditions.
ww.An agent's duty to act for a principal a: An agent's duty to a principal belongs to agency law, whereas premises liability is a tort doctrine about injuries on someone's property.
ww.A tax on buildings charged by the city e: A building tax is a government charge, but premises liability concerns an owner's responsibility for injuries on the property.

rw: A store that knew of a broken stair for weeks and failed to repair or warn breached its duty of care to customers under premises liability, so it is likely liable.

ww.Only a tax penalty paid by the owner: A tax penalty is unrelated to the customer's injury; the store faces a negligence claim for a hazard it knew about and failed to fix.
ww.Full immunity from any civil liability: Stores have no immunity from civil liability for known hazards, and a customer injured by a known defect can sue for damages.
ww.No liability because customers should lo: Customers can expect reasonably safe premises, and a store that knew about a hazard for weeks cannot rely on customers to avoid it.

rw: A nuisance is an unreasonable interference with another's use and enjoyment of land, such as noise, odors or pollution, and may support damages or an injunction.

ww.A tax on land charged by the local count: A land tax is a government charge, and a nuisance is a tort claim about interference with use of land.
ww.A contract term that sets the price of g: A price term in a sales contract is part of a contract, whereas a nuisance is a tort about interfering with land use.
ww.A friendly neighbor who helps out with c: A helpful neighbor is not a legal nuisance; the tort concerns unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of land.

rw: Trespass is the unauthorized entry onto another person's land, or causing something to enter it, and it is an intentional tort even without harm.

ww.A fair trade deal between two firms: A fair trade deal is a lawful commercial agreement, while trespass is an unauthorized entry onto another's land.
ww.A loan default by a borrower to a bank: A loan default is a breach of a financial obligation, and trespass is an intentional tort involving entry onto land.
ww.A zoning rule for the use of the land: A zoning rule regulates land use, whereas trespass is the tort of entering another's land without permission.

rw: Tortious interference occurs when a person intentionally and improperly causes someone to breach a contract with another party, harming the other party.

ww.Giving advice to a firm about how it sho: Giving advice to a firm is lawful consulting and does not induce a breach of a contract with another party.
ww.Signing a contract with a supplier for t: Signing a supplier contract is a normal lawful transaction, with no interference with someone else's contract.
ww.Paying a bill to a supplier on the due d: Paying a bill on time is performing a contract, not interfering with one, so it cannot be a tort.

rw: Bribing a supplier to break its contract with a rival intentionally induces a breach, which is tortious interference with contract.

ww.Negligence in the way it was done: Negligence involves carelessness, while the competitor acted intentionally to cause the supplier's breach, so tortious interference fits better.
ww.Defamation of the supplier's name: Defamation concerns false statements harming reputation, and the facts here involve a bribe to induce a breach.
ww.Nuisance caused by the competitor: Nuisance is interference with land use, whereas here the competitor induced a contract breach through a bribe.

rw: The three U.S. patent types are utility patents for new inventions, design patents for ornamental appearance and plant patents for new asexually reproduced plants.

ww.Food, drink and tobacco: Food, drink and tobacco are products and are not patent categories, which are utility, design and plant patents.
ww.Red, white and blue shades: Colors are not patent types; the three U.S. types are utility, design and plant, protecting function, ornamental design and new plant varieties.
ww.Land, sea and air patents: Land, sea and air are not patent categories; U.S. patents are utility, design and plant.

rw: A design patent protects the new, original, ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture, not how it works, and lasts 15 years from grant.

ww.How a product works and functions: How a product works and functions is protected by a utility patent, not a design patent.
ww.A brand name and logo for a firm: Brand names and logos are protected by trademarks, while a design patent protects the ornamental look of an article.
ww.A secret recipe kept by the company: A secret recipe is typically protected as a trade secret and not by a patent, which requires public disclosure.

rw: A design patent protects the ornamental appearance of an article, so the distinctive chair shape is best covered by it.

ww.A chair copyright: Copyright protects creative expression and does not typically protect the useful shape of an article like a chair, so it is a weak fit.
ww.A trademark only: A trademark identifies the source of goods, and it would not best protect the chair's ornamental shape by itself.
ww.A utility patent: A utility patent protects how an invention works, not how it looks, so it does not best cover a chair's appearance.

rw: For works created by an individual today, U.S. copyright generally lasts for the author's life plus 70 years after death.

ww.Twenty years from first filing: Twenty years from filing is the term of a utility patent, not copyright, which generally lasts far longer.
ww.One year after first publication: One year is far too short; copyright subsists from creation and generally lasts the author's life plus 70 years.
ww.Five years after publication: Five years after publication is far shorter than copyright's actual term of the author's life plus 70 years.

rw: The DMCA creates a notice-and-takedown process for removing infringing online content and gives platforms safe harbor from liability if they comply.

ww.Taxes the sales of digital goods and ser: Sales taxes on digital goods are governed by state tax law and the DMCA is a copyright statute.
ww.Sets the federal minimum wage and overti: Minimum wage and overtime rules come from the Fair Labor Standards Act, and the DMCA addresses digital copyright.
ww.Regulates the safety standards for cars: Car safety standards are set by federal motor vehicle regulators, whereas the DMCA concerns copyright in digital works.

rw: Trade dress is the overall look and feel of a product or its packaging that identifies its source, protected under trademark law if it is distinctive and nonfunctional.

ww.A tax form that a business files each ye: A tax form reports sales and income to the government, while trade dress is a form of trademark protection for a product's look.
ww.A shipping label that shows the address: A shipping label identifies the sender and buyer, whereas trade dress identifies the source of a product by its overall appearance.
ww.Clothing worn by workers at a shop or a: Worker clothing is a uniform, and trade dress is a trademark concept covering the overall appearance of a product or packaging.

rw: Copying a famous chain's decor, uniforms and layout in a confusing way can be trade dress infringement under the Lanham Act.

ww.Respondeat superior only: Respondeat superior makes employers liable for employees' acts and does not address copying a chain's distinctive look.
ww.Breach of warranty claim: Breach of warranty concerns promises about goods and does not address copying of a restaurant's overall look.
ww.Statute of frauds claim: The statute of frauds concerns which contracts must be in writing and has no bearing on copying a chain's appearance.

rw: Cybersquatting is registering a domain name that matches a famous brand in bad faith to profit by reselling it, and it is addressed by the ACPA.

ww.Tax planning: Tax planning is arranging finances to reduce taxes and has no connection to registering famous brand names to profit.
ww.Franchising: Franchising is licensing a business model to operators, a legitimate arrangement unrelated to bad faith domain registrations.
ww.Telemarketing: Telemarketing is selling by phone and has no connection to domain name disputes.

rw: Diversity jurisdiction lets federal courts hear cases between citizens of different states when more than $75,000 is at stake, which prevents local bias.

ww.Authority over sports leagues and the ru: Sports leagues set their own rules, and diversity jurisdiction is a federal court power over disputes between citizens of different states.
ww.Authority over cultural groups and the w: Cultural groups are not a subject of federal jurisdiction, while diversity jurisdiction concerns parties from different states.
ww.Authority over disputes among employees: Disputes among employees and managers in a firm are not diversity cases, which require citizens of different states and an amount in controversy.

rw: Ohio and Texas citizens are diverse parties and $200,000 exceeds $75,000, so a federal district court has diversity jurisdiction.

ww.Small claims court only, whatever the su: Small claims court handles low-dollar disputes, and a $200,000 claim exceeds typical limits, so small claims is not the right court.
ww.The Supreme Court as the court of first: The Supreme Court hears cases mainly on appeal and has original jurisdiction only in narrow cases, not an ordinary contract dispute.
ww.No court can hear the case, as the sum i: Plenty of courts can hear it: state courts, or federal court under diversity, and a large sum does not remove jurisdiction.

rw: Venue is the proper geographic location for a trial, usually where the parties live or the dispute arose, and it may be changed for fairness.

ww.The judge's salary, paid out of the budg: A judge's salary is a budget matter and has nothing to do with venue, which concerns the location of trial.
ww.The jury's size and the number of its me: Jury size is set by procedural rules, whereas venue refers to the geographic location of the trial.
ww.The lawyer's fee and how it is to be pai: Lawyer fees are set by agreement or statute, while venue is the geographic location of the trial.

rw: A motion to dismiss asks the court to end a case because the complaint fails to state a legally sufficient claim, even if all alleged facts are true.

ww.A request for a bigger jury to hear the: A larger jury is a trial matter, while a motion to dismiss asks the court to end the case for a legal defect.
ww.A request to change the judge's name on: Changing a judge's name makes no legal sense; a motion to dismiss asks the court to end the case because the claim is legally insufficient.
ww.A request to add more parties to the cas: Adding parties is done by a motion to join or intervene, whereas a motion to dismiss ends the case.

rw: Summary judgment asks the court to rule for one side as a matter of law when no genuine dispute of material fact exists.

ww.Motion to appeal: A motion to appeal is not a trial court motion on facts; an appeal asks a higher court to review a final decision.
ww.Motion in limine: A motion in limine asks the court to exclude certain evidence before or during trial, not to decide the case.
ww.Motion to compel: A motion to compel asks the court to force a party to comply with discovery requests and does not decide the case.

rw: A verdict is the jury's decision on the facts of a case, such as finding the defendant liable or not liable.

ww.The list of witnesses called by each sid: A witness list names the people who will testify and is not the decision of the jury.
ww.The court's schedule of hearings this ye: A court schedule sets hearing dates and is not the decision on the facts, which is the verdict.
ww.The lawyer's fee for the work on the cas: A lawyer's fee is a cost for legal services and is not a decision by the jury about the case.

rw: Appellate courts review the record for legal errors in the lower court, and they usually defer to the trial court's findings of fact.

ww.New witnesses from scratch in a fresh tr: Appellate courts generally do not hear new witnesses or hold a fresh trial; they review the record from the lower court.
ww.The jury's names and home addresses on f: Juror names and addresses are not what an appeals court reviews; it examines the trial record for legal errors.
ww.The lawyers' fashion and the clothes the: Lawyers' clothing is irrelevant to appeals, which focus on legal errors in the lower court's proceedings.

rw: A default judgment is entered for the plaintiff when the defendant fails to respond or appear after being properly served with the complaint.

ww.A settlement reached by both sides befor: A pretrial settlement is an agreement between the sides, whereas a default judgment is entered when a defendant fails to respond.
ww.A judgment for the defendant when the pl: A default judgment is not for the defendant when the plaintiff dies; it favors the plaintiff when the defendant does not respond.
ww.A jury's apology to the parties after a: An apology from a jury is not a legal judgment; a default judgment results from a defendant's failure to respond.
